articles.title: Así de directo habla el doctor Pedro Cavadas de la muerte con pacientes: "Jamás le miento"
articles.standfirst: Reflexiones que se han hecho virales por la forma de detallarlo bajo un concepto que aplica en casos determinados como la cercanía de la muerte en pacientes
articles.summary: Reflexiones que se han hecho virales por la forma de detallarlo bajo un concepto que aplica en casos determinados como la cercanía de la muerte en pacientes
articles.body: El doctor Pedro Cavadas es uno de los médicos más mediáticos de España por sus intervenciones y ha vuelto a la escena tras no hacerlo de forma tan habitual hacía tiempo. El cirujano dejaba reflexiones profundas en su visita al nuevo programa de Cristina Pardo 'La Mesa' que se han hecho virales. No tiene reparos en decirle a alguien que su enfermedad no tiene cura. "Un principio básico que sigo es: jamás le miento a un paciente salvo que crea que se va a morir muy pronto. Creo que es razonable y es beneficioso contar una mentira piadosa a un paciente que sabes que va a durar nada", ha señalado al respecto de su estilo de trabajo. Se ha centrado en sus pacientes que acuden a sus manos por sufrir tumores en la cabeza y el cuello "que son muy desfigurantes" e impiden cosas básicas como comer o tragar, es decir, impiden socializar. "No son curables pero tienen mejoría con cirugía. Siempre les digo: ¿quiere que le diga la verdad o no? Alguien de la familia tiene que saber la verdad. Normalmente el paciente quiere saber la verdad". De hecho, Cavadas explicaba a sus pacientes cuando ya no hay solución que la "única diferencia entre usted y yo es que usted sabe la causa de su muerte, yo no sé cuál va a ser la mía. Usted sabemos más o menos cuándo se va a morir. Yo no sé cuándo me voy a morir. Podría morir antes que usted". Y añadía que "con una cirugía bien hecha", que encima no le quitaría mucho tiempo personal, puede conseguir que muchas personas "lleven una vida digna" y que un enfermo "hable, pueda tragar, que sea visible y que pueda morir en buenas condiciones".

articles.title: A generation cannot remember 9/11. We have a duty to make sure they learn
articles.summary: The 9/11 Memorial & Museum is bringing student workshops, lesson plans and digital learning to ensure over 100 million post-9/11 Americans never forget.
articles.body: After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, this country made an enduring promise to "Never Forget." It was a promise made by those of us who witnessed the attacks. Twenty-five years later, it is now a promise we must pass down to those born since 9/11. More than 100 million Americans are too young to remember 9/11. They know 9/11 as a moment in history books rather than a day that began with clear skies that were soon darkened by smoke and fear. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS These 100 million Americans are not all children. They are now firefighters and police officers. They are enlisted service members and officers carrying out missions reshaped by the 9/11 attacks. They are parents, neighbors and volunteers. And a great many of them now stand in classrooms as teachers and role models for our youth. To put this in perspective, students starting high school this fall were born over a decade after the attacks. They might also be taught by someone too young to remember 9/11 or who wasn't even born yet. 9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY A quarter-century on, that is the challenge before this country, and it is addressed by the work we do every day at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum: making sure the promise to never forget does not fade. Since the museum opened in 2014, more than 28 million visitors have passed through its doors. Increasingly, they come to learn what happened here because they didn't live through it themselves. Inside, visitors see the names, faces, and stories of the 2,977 victims. They see the things people carried that morning, like business cards and wallets. They take in the scale of the twisted steel from the towers. And they learn about what happened from the stories and firsthand accounts of people there that day. They also experience the spirit of Sept. 12 and learn how our city, country and world came together in ways big and small in the aftermath of tragedy. Neighbors raised flags in solidarity. Volunteers came to Ground Zero to help any way they could. Schoolchildren visited their local firehouses. On Sept. 12, 2001, and afterward, we witnessed some of the very best of our country's resilience, caring and patriotism. People from more than 90 countries were killed, and people came from all over the world to help. MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA But we know not everyone can come to us in lower Manhattan to see these artifacts, hear these stories and experience the memorial and museum. That is why we at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum are committed to bringing the legacy of Sept. 11 to students everywhere. We have developed student workshops, online programs, lesson plans and professional development opportunities to ensure educators are empowered and equipped to teach this subject. 9/11 STEEL BEAM ARRIVES AT FLORIDA SCHOOL WHERE BUSH LEARNED AMERICA WAS UNDER ATTACK Every summer, teachers come to lower Manhattan from across the country to spend a few days with us. They walk the museum floor, hear firsthand accounts and interact with experts. Many of them were in school that morning and some weren't born yet. They come because they know a textbook won't be enough when they stand in front of a classroom in September. They go home with the essential resources and a better sense of how to teach something that is still lived history. A quarter-century on, that is the challenge before this country, and it is addressed by the work we do every day at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum: making sure the promise to never forget does not fade. This year, as we commemorate the 25th anniversary of the attacks, we encourage you to take time to learn about 9/11 and to share stories of hope and community that are part of its legacy. It's our duty to educate future generations and help them understand not only the scope of that tragic day but also the acts of service, compassion, and courage that it inspired. If you're a student, join our Anniversary Digital Learning Experience, ask questions and listen to those who lived through this day, whether that's family, neighbors or recorded videos and interviews.
